title: EU Hits Google With $1 Billion Fine as US Threatens Tariff Retaliation
excerpt: The European Commission fined Alphabet's Google €890 million for breaching the Digital Markets Act — the tech giant's first penalties under the landmark law — as U.S. lawmakers call for trade retaliation over Europe's tech regulations.
body:
The European Commission fined Alphabet's Google a total of €890 million ($1.02 billion) on Thursday for violating rules designed to curb Big Tech's dominance, marking the company's first penalties under the bloc's three-year-old Digital Markets Act.

The decision underscored Brussels' determination to enforce its digital competition laws even as the Trump administration and U.S. legislators escalate pressure against what they call discriminatory targeting of American technology companies.

Two Fines, Two Violations

The larger fine of €460 million targeted Google's practice of giving its own shopping, hotel, transportation, and sports services preferential placement in Google Search results over rival offerings. A second fine of €430 million addressed restrictions on Google Play that prevented app developers from steering users to cheaper offers on competing app stores or websites.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GRHdPwsoP8A

"The best products should succeed because they're better, not because they're owned by the company running the search engine."

— Teresa Ribera, European Commission Executive Vice President for Competition Policy

"We found that Google harms businesses offering similar services, such as shopping or sports, by not granting them the same level of prominence on Google Search," said Henna Virkkunen, the EU commissioner in charge of tech sovereignty. Google has 60 days to comply with orders to treat rivals fairly.

Google Pushes Back

Google criticized the findings and signaled it may challenge them in court. Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, accused the Commission of forcing the company to degrade its products.

"To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love — like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants — and dismantle safety protections on Google Play."

— Kent Walker, Google President of Global Affairs

Walker called the enforcement "product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit."

Caught in the Tariff Crossfire

The fines land at a fraught moment in transatlantic relations. A group of 25 U.S. lawmakers wrote to President Trump this week urging him to use "all available tools," including tariff investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, to retaliate against EU tech regulations.

The timing is particularly charged because new tariffs are expected to replace temporary levies that expire on Friday. The Trump administration has repeatedly characterized European tech fines as trade barriers targeting American firms.

Ribera dismissed suggestions that political considerations influenced the decision. "We are bound by the law," she said. "I don't think that any of us could be respected if we could decide whether to do or not to do because someone else is trying to tell us what to do."

A Decade of Fines — and What Comes Next

Thursday's fines are the third DMA enforcement action, following penalties against Apple and Meta Platforms in April 2025. For Google, they bring total EU antitrust fines to €10.38 billion across six cases — a figure that could grow through follow-on damages claims in national courts across Europe.

The Commission did signal a path toward de-escalation, noting Google has proposed and begun testing changes to how it presents its own services in search results. EU regulators called these developments "good progress towards compliance" and indicated daily penalties for non-compliance are likely off the table.

In a notable expansion of the DMA's reach, regulators said the principles from Thursday's decision could also apply to Google's AI-generated summaries — AI Overviews and AI Mode — with further discussions expected on how the law governs those features.
image_caption: Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's executive vice president for competition policy, announced the €890 million fine against Google. The decision marks the first DMA penalties for the tech giant amid rising U.S.-EU trade tensions.
nri_angle: EU tech regulation sets precedent that could affect Indian IT companies operating in Europe and shapes the global regulatory landscape for Big Tech.
